newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Suicide bomber kills two, self in Tel Aviv cafe.
newsitem.headline: Suicide bomber kills two, self in Tel Aviv cafe.

text.p: A suspected Moslem suicide bomber killed two people in a crowded cafe in Tel Aviv on Friday, dealing another blow to faltering Middle East peacemaking.
The blast ripped through the outdoor terrace where families were relaxing at lunchtime ahead of the Jewish Sabbath holiday.
Half-finished meals lay on the few wooden tables that escaped the full force of the explosion at the Apropos cafe on central Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Street.
The attack came amid heightened Israeli-Palestinian tension over the groundbreaking on Tuesday of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Police said three people were killed, including the suspected bomber, and 43 were wounded.
At the scene, an Israeli policewoman cradled a baby girl in her arms, looking for the crying infant's parents. The baby wore the tatters of a clown costume for the Jewish Purim festival.
"I saw her mother," medic Pinni Melech told Israel Radio. "Her whole face was burned, without an ear and a mess."
Mother and child were taken to Tel Aviv's Ichilov hospital -- the baby to intensive care. The hospital would not comment on the mother's fate.

It was a scene reminiscent of Tel Aviv one year ago when a Hamas suicide bomber killed 13 people in a shopping mall at the time of the Purim festival. The blast also came just over a week after seven Israeli schoolgirls were shot dead at the Jordan River by a Jordanian soldier.
"It was a terribly big explosion, the windows shattered to pieces," said waitress Iris Gan. "I saw a woman lying on the ground covered with blood, being dragged to the ambulance."
Police Commissioner Assaf Hefetz said: "There was a terrorist who blew himself up, apparently, a bomb, not very big."
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat condemned Friday's explosion as a "terrorist incident".
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Arafat's Palestinian Authority of indirectly giving a green light to attackers.

"I said these organisations understood from the things that were said to them they had the approval of the Palestinian Authority...There is no doubt they acted on the basis of that understanding," he told reporters while visiting wounded in hospital.

He was referring to Islamic fundamentalist organisations such as Hamas which carried out suicide bombings last year in an attempt to torpedo the Palestinian self-rule agreement with Israel which it sees as a sellout of Palestinian rights.
An anonymous telephone caller told police that the Hamas group carried out the attack.
Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani rejected Netanyahu's accusation that the Authority had sanctioned violence, pinning the blame on the Israeli leader's settlement policy.

"It's a shame that the Israeli prime minister lies in front his people and holds President Arafat responsible," Kanafani told reporters. "The person ultimately responsible for this painful deed is Netanyahu himself, who did not listen to the advice of the international community."

Netanyahu did not say he would halt peace talks with the Palestinians, who have accused the right-wing Israeli leader of fomenting unrest by forging ahead with the settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim or Har Homa, southeast of Jerusalem.
Israeli security chiefs issued warnings of possible unrest on Friday, the traditional day for Moslem prayers, over Har Homa, but the army was on alert mainly in the West Bank.

Netanyahu clamped a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip after the bombing, preventing Palestinian workers entering Israel. But hundreds of Palestinian youths clashed with Israelis soldiers in Hebron on Friday.
In Gaza, Palestinian police prevented a rally by Hamas after news of the attack. Hamas claimed responsibility for a wave of suicide attacks last year that killed 59 people in Israel.
In Helsinki, a White House official condemned the bombing and said U.S. President Bill Clinton, attending a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin, would speak out against it.
A radical Palestinian group said Netanyahu should expect more attacks because he was rejecting peace with Arabs.

"As long as there is occupation and (Jewish) settlements over Arab lands, Netanyahu should expect Palestinians to defend themselves with all means and to launch more confrontations," Maher al-Taher, spokesman for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, said in Damascus.
